name: Rare-event calibration and PR-AUC vs ROC-AUC; pooled vs within-unit AUC. Core sources: Saito & Rehmsmeier (2015) 'The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot When Evaluating Binary Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets'; Davis & Goadrich (2006) 'The Relationship Between Precision-Recall and ROC Curves'; Boyd, Santos Costa, Davis & Page (2012) 'Unachievable Region in Precision-Recall Space and Its Effect on Empirical Evaluation'; Flach & Kull (2015) 'Precision-Recall-Gain Curves: PR Analysis Done Right'; McDermott, Zhang, Hansen, Angelotti & Gallifant (2024) 'A Closer Look at AUROC and AUPRC under Class Imbalance'; van Klaveren, Steyerberg, Perel & Vergouwe (2014) 'Assessing discriminative ability of risk models in clustered data'; Michael & Tian 'The Population and Personalized Areas Under the ROC Curve' (Statistica Sinica); Janes & Pepe (2008/2009) covariate-adjusted ROC; Hand (2009) H-measure; Van Calster et al. (2016) calibration hierarchy; van den Goorbergh et al. (2022) harm of class-imbalance corrections; Wilks (2010) Brier score sampling under serial dependence.

popularity: Saito & Rehmsmeier 2015 and Davis & Goadrich 2006 are among the most cited papers on imbalanced-classification evaluation (several thousand citations each) [uncertain: counts not retrieved in this session]. McDermott et al. report reviewing over 1.5 million papers and finding the 'AUPRC is better under imbalance' claim often uncited or misattributed. van Klaveren 2014 and Van Calster 2016 are standard references in clinical prediction modelling. Citation counts for the others were not retrieved.
peer_review_status: peer-reviewed: PLoS ONE (Saito), ICML (Davis & Goadrich; Boyd), NeurIPS (Flach & Kull; McDermott), BMC Med Res Methodol (van Klaveren), Statistica Sinica (Michael & Tian), Am J Epidemiol / Biometrika (Janes & Pepe), Machine Learning (Hand), J Clin Epidemiol (Van Calster), JAMIA (van den Goorbergh), QJRMS (Wilks). Baddeley et al. 2025 is an arXiv preprint.
target_type: Generic binary event; not an air-alert application. The metric issues bite hardest on our ONSET target with an at-risk mask: masking removes the easy 'already under alert' rows, so discrimination must come from genuinely predicting new starts. A state target would raise every metric (ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and Brier skill against a weak reference) through persistence, which none of these metrics flags by itself.
target_definition: Generic: Y in {0,1}, score or probability p. For the project: y(t) = 1 if a new alert starts in (t, t+H], H = 1 h (H = 3 h in reports/official_h3), on unmasked oblast-hours only. Project base rates from reports/official/metrics_validation.csv (validation [2026-06-29, 2026-07-27)): overall 0.118 (1,316 positives of 11,160 rows). From reports/official/metrics.csv (6-week final test, first accessed 2026-10-13 per reports/final_test_access.json): overall 0.139, Kyiv City 0.123, frontline 0.479, rear 0.088. So this is a MODERATELY imbalanced problem overall, with very different prevalence across groups. The cross-group prevalence spread matters more for metric choice than the overall imbalance.
spatial_unit: Not applicable in the method papers. The clustered-AUC papers treat 'cluster' generically (hospital centres in van Klaveren; police districts or areas in Michael & Tian's urban policing application). For us: cluster = oblast (24 units minus exclusions), with groups Kyiv City / frontline / rear.
at_risk_masking: Not applicable in the papers. For us: all metrics must be computed on exactly the same unmasked rows for the model and all baselines (src/evaluate.py metric_table already does this). The mask changes prevalence per oblast in a way that depends on how often the oblast is under alert. Frontline oblasts lose most of their hours to the mask, and the remaining at-risk hours have a base rate near 0.48. This makes PR-AUC levels not comparable across groups.
data_sources: Method papers with their own illustrations: Saito & Rehmsmeier use simulated imbalanced data plus a re-analysis of bioinformatics (microRNA gene discovery) classifiers [uncertain: exact case-study details not re-checked]. McDermott et al. use synthetic data (subgroup prevalences 0.05 vs 0.01) and real fairness datasets (adult, compas, lsac, mimic). van Klaveren 2014 uses the CRASH trial: 2,081 traumatic-brain-injury patients in 35 centres. van den Goorbergh 2022 use Monte Carlo simulation plus an ovarian-cancer case study. Michael & Tian use urban policing data. Project numbers cited here come from reports/official/metrics_validation.csv and reports/official/metrics.csv in this repo.
data_source_variant: Not applicable (no air-alert data in the sources). Project numbers are from the official Vadimkin dataset only (D-007), with no mixing with API data.
preprocessing: Not applicable. Metric-computation note: scikit-learn average_precision_score computes AP = sum_n (R_n - R_{n-1}) P_n, a step-wise sum with no interpolation, which the docs contrast with trapezoidal area under the PR curve as 'too optimistic'. Davis & Goadrich show that linear interpolation in PR space is invalid. So the project's 'PR-AUC' is AP (CLAUDE.md already says PR-AUC = average precision), and it should never be computed with sklearn.metrics.auc(recall, precision).
known_label_artefacts: Metric artefacts rather than label artefacts: (1) Ties. Tie-heavy forecasters (raw persistence 0/1, climatology with 168 values per oblast, the shrunken recent rate) get ROC-AUC with ties counted as 0.5 and AP with tied scores grouped into one threshold [uncertain: sklearn tie grouping inferred from precision_recall_curve behaviour, not quoted from the docs]. Raw persistence's low AUC is partly a tie effect. (2) The within-unit eligibility filter. The project's within-unit mean ROC-AUC uses only units with >= 10 positives and >= 10 negatives (src/config.py min_class_per_unit). On validation this excluded 10 of 24 units (chernivetska, dnipropetrovska, ivano_frankivska, kharkivska, khmelnytska, lvivska, rivnenska, ternopilska, volynska, zakarpatska), and on the final test 8. The excluded set mixes quiet western oblasts (too few positives) and Dnipropetrovska / Kharkivska (too few at-risk rows). So the within-unit mean describes a selected subset, which must be stated next to the number. (3) Prevalence floor. Boyd et al. show that part of PR space is unachievable and that the minimum AUCPR depends only on class skew, so raw PR-AUC carries a free component that grows with base rate.
model_family: Evaluation methods, not models. (1) ROC-AUC = P(score of a random positive > score of a random negative). It is invariant to prevalence and to any monotone transform, so it ignores calibration. (2) PR-AUC / average precision: depends on prevalence. A random classifier's precision equals the base rate, and the unachievable-region floor rises with skew (Boyd 2012). PR-Gain (Flach & Kull 2015) rescales precision and recall against the always-positive baseline to give a universal baseline. (3) McDermott et al. 2024, Theorem 1: AUROC = 1 - E[FPR at positive scores], while AUPRC = 1 - P(y=0) E[FPR / firing rate], so AUPRC up-weights false positives at high thresholds. Theorem 2: AUROC rewards fixing any misordered pair equally, while AUPRC rewards fixes at high scores more. Theorem 3: under calibration and a large prevalence gap between subgroups, the fix that most raises AUPRC lies inside the HIGH-prevalence subgroup. (4) Clustered AUC: between-cluster vs within-cluster concordance (van Klaveren 2014), and population vs personalized AUC (Michael & Tian), which can diverge in either direction (Simpson-type paradox). (5) Covariate-adjusted ROC, AROC (Janes & Pepe): a weighted average of covariate-specific ROC curves, i.e. ROC conditional on the stratifier. (6) H-measure (Hand 2009): AUC implicitly averages misclassification costs with a model-dependent weight. H uses a fixed Beta prior over costs; Hand & Anagnostopoulos suggest Beta(pi1+1, pi0+1) for unbalanced data. (7) Calibration hierarchy (Van Calster 2016): mean (calibration-in-the-large), weak (logistic intercept 0 and slope 1), moderate (event rate R% among forecasts of R%), strong (calibrated for every covariate pattern). They prove moderate calibration guarantees non-harmful decisions.
features: Not applicable (no forecasting features). Implementation pieces for the project: sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score and average_precision_score (already used in src/evaluate.py); a groupby('unit') loop for within-unit ROC-AUC (already present, unweighted mean); optionally the same loop for within-unit AP and AP / unit base rate; optionally a groupby('t') loop for a cross-sectional 'within-hour' AUC that ranks oblasts against each other at the same forecast time (an interpretation added here, not from a source). No new dependency is needed.
ablation_design: Not applicable in the sources. Implication: feature ablations should be judged on Brier / BSS and within-unit AUC on identical rows. Pooled ROC-AUC barely moves for features that only add within-oblast timing signal, because it is dominated by between-oblast separation.
split_scheme: Not applicable. Wilks (2010): serial correlation inflates the sampling variance of the Brier score and BSS, so iid confidence intervals are too narrow and p-values too small. The same applies to AUC and AP computed on hourly, clustered rows.
metrics: ROC-AUC (pooled, within-cluster, covariate-adjusted), PR-AUC / average precision (raw, relative to prevalence, PR-Gain), H-measure, calibration-in-the-large, calibration intercept and slope, moderate-calibration (reliability) curves, Brier score and Brier skill score.
unit_of_metric: This is the core issue. A pooled AUC over oblast-hours mixes (a) between-oblast separation (frontline vs rear), (b) between-period separation within an oblast (active vs quiet weeks), and (c) hour-to-hour timing. The project's own numbers show it. Validation: model pooled ROC-AUC 0.884 vs within-unit mean 0.606; rolling recent-rate pooled 0.883 vs within-unit 0.491; climatology 0.850 vs 0.516; calibrated persistence 0.881 vs 0.588. Final test: model 0.875 vs 0.632; recent-rate 0.870 vs 0.491. A 14-day rolling rate is nearly constant within an oblast over a few weeks, so it ranks at chance within an oblast, yet it matches the model on pooled AUC. Pooled AUC here mostly measures 'which oblast is busy', as the outline note says. Within-group (rear) numbers repeat the pattern (final test: model pooled 0.878 vs within 0.642), because rear oblasts also differ a lot in base rate.
baseline_strength: Not applicable in the sources. For the project, the pooled-vs-within gap is itself a baseline diagnostic. A forecaster whose pooled AUC is near the model's but whose within-unit AUC is near 0.5 (recent-rate) shows that pooled AUC cannot separate the model from a per-oblast constant. Brier skill vs the rolling recent rate (D-021) is the right headline. On it, the model is at -0.0097 on validation and -0.010 on the final test overall, i.e. it does NOT beat recent-rate on the primary metric while still winning on within-unit AUC (0.606-0.632 vs 0.491). This is a reportable 'better ranking within oblasts, slightly worse overall Brier' result.
calibration: Van Calster 2016: aim for moderate calibration (reliability curve). Strong calibration is unrealistic. Calibration-in-the-large is the weakest level, but it is the first thing to break under drift. For the project, reports/official/calibrator.json records decision 'none' with validation ECE 0.0123, so no recalibrator was fitted. van den Goorbergh 2022: random undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE all caused strong over-estimation of minority-class probability with no gain in AUROC, and the over-estimation could not always be fixed by recalibration. The model uses plain objective 'binary' in src/model.py with no scale_pos_weight / is_unbalance, which is consistent with that advice. King & Zeng (2001, Political Analysis), from the conflict literature, show logistic regression under-estimates rare-event probabilities in small samples [uncertain: cited from memory, not re-checked this session]. At our base rates (about 0.09-0.48 per group) this small-sample bias is minor.
calibration_under_drift: Not addressed directly by the discrimination papers. In the calibration hierarchy, calibration-in-the-large (mean predicted - observed) is the level that drifts first under a base-rate shift, and ROC-AUC is blind to it. Project final-test calibration-in-the-large (reports/official/calibration_in_the_large.csv): model -0.006 overall, but -0.075 frontline, -0.030 Kyiv City and +0.006 rear. The overall number hides group-level miscalibration of opposite sign, so calibration-in-the-large must be reported per group (as D-015 (c) already requires for the new regime). PR-AUC also shifts mechanically with base rate (Boyd 2012), so before/after-reform PR-AUC differences must be read through PR-AUC / base rate or PR-Gain, not raw AP.
uncertainty_of_gain: Wilks 2010: serial dependence inflates the variance of Brier and BSS, so iid intervals are too narrow. van Klaveren 2014: cluster-specific c-indexes vary a lot (IQR 0.70-0.81 across 35 centres), and they recommend pooling them by meta-analysis (fixed or random effects) to get a summary and a heterogeneity estimate. The 2019 paper warns that c-indexes in small clusters are too extreme and proposes a calibrated model-based concordance. For the project: within-unit AUCs from units with only 10-30 positives in a 4-6 week window are noisy. Report the spread (or a week-block bootstrap, D-013) together with the mean.
regime_coverage: Not applicable (no alert data). Note: McDermott's Theorem 3 matters for regime comparisons. After the yellow/red reform the per-oblast prevalence pattern changes, so pooled AP shifts toward whatever subgroup became higher-prevalence, independent of model quality.
leakage_handling: Not a leakage topic in the sources, but three metric-hygiene risks are leakage-like: (1) Normalising PR-AUC by the TEST base rate is fine as a descriptive ratio, but a 'prevalence-adjusted' score must not be fed back into model selection on test. (2) Choosing min_class_per_unit, the set of units, or the weighting of the within-unit mean after seeing test numbers is a forking-paths risk. Fix them in the pre-registration (reports/official/preregistration.json exists for that). (3) Any fitted recalibration (Platt or isotonic) must be fitted on validation and applied to the frozen model (D-021), never fitted on test rows. Diagnostic calibration curves on test are fine.
test_window_hygiene: Not applicable in the sources. Project: final-test metrics were first accessed 2026-10-13T00:16:53Z with SHA-256 hashes of the pre-registration (reports/final_test_access.json). The within-unit AUC definition (unweighted mean, >= 10 pos and >= 10 neg) is in src/config.py and predates that access [uncertain: commit ordering not checked]. Any new metric added now (within-unit AP, PR-Gain, within-hour AUC) is post hoc on the test window and must be labelled as such in the README.
headline_results: (1) Saito & Rehmsmeier 2015: on imbalanced data, ROC plots can look reassuring because low FPR is cheap when negatives dominate. PR plots show how often a positive call is right, so they are more informative for practical use. (2) Davis & Goadrich 2006: a curve dominates in ROC space iff it dominates in PR space. Linear interpolation in PR space is invalid. Optimising AUROC does not guarantee optimising AUPRC. (3) Boyd 2012: a skew-dependent unachievable region gives every classifier some AUCPR 'for free', so AUCPR is not comparable across different class balances. (4) Flach & Kull 2015: PR-Gain curves give a universal baseline, and the area under ordinary PR curves can favour models with lower expected F1. (5) McDermott et al. 2024: AUPRC is NOT generally superior under class imbalance. It prioritises high-score errors and, under prevalence differences, improvements in the high-prevalence subgroup (synthetic case: subgroup prevalences 0.05 vs 0.01; optimising AUPRC widened the AUROC gap between groups, optimising AUROC raised both; on real data the effect tracked the prevalence gap, Spearman rho = 0.905, p = 0.002). Recommendation: AUROC for context-independent evaluation and allocation across subpopulations, AUPRC for single-population, top-of-list retrieval; report both. (6) van Klaveren 2014: within-cluster concordance is the relevant quantity when decisions are taken within a cluster; cluster-specific c-indexes in CRASH varied, IQR 0.70-0.81, pooled 0.76 (95% CI 0.66-0.82) [uncertain: whether 0.76 (0.66-0.82) is the pooled estimate or a prediction interval was not re-checked]. (7) Michael & Tian: population and personalized (within-cluster) AUCs can diverge strongly, and the paper gives joint estimation and inference. (8) Van Calster 2016: four-level calibration hierarchy; moderate calibration guarantees non-harmful decisions. (9) van den Goorbergh 2022: imbalance corrections cause over-estimation of risk without improving AUROC. (10) Project illustration (validation): pooled ROC-AUC model 0.884 vs recent-rate 0.883 (no separation), within-unit model 0.606 vs recent-rate 0.491 (clear separation), Brier skill vs recent-rate -0.0097. PR-AUC / base rate: model 3.95 vs recent-rate 4.11.
code_available: Yes, for what the project needs: scikit-learn (already pinned) has roc_auc_score and average_precision_score. Within-unit AUC is in src/evaluate.py within_unit_auc. Optional extras would need a new dependency and the human's approval: hmeasure (R/Python), prg (Flach's PR-Gain code, linked from https://www.cs.bris.ac.uk/~flach/PRGcurves/), reliabilitydiag (R). PR-Gain and within-unit AP are a few lines each without any dependency.
takeaways_for_project:
1) Treat pooled ROC-AUC as a between-oblast metric, not a skill metric. Our own validation numbers show recent-rate tying the model on pooled AUC (0.883 vs 0.884) while ranking at chance within oblasts (0.491 vs 0.606). The README should say so explicitly and lead discrimination results with the within-unit mean AUC (CLAUDE.md already requires both). [Interpretation: the gap comes mainly from between-oblast base-rate differences plus slow between-week variation.]
2) Keep Brier skill vs rolling recent-rate (D-021) as the headline. Neither AUC nor PR-AUC is a proper score or sensitive to calibration, and both are rank-based. The current result (BSS about -0.01 overall, positive in Kyiv City +0.074 on the test) should be reported as 'does not beat recent-rate on the primary metric overall' (D-021 says this is valid and reportable), with within-unit AUC as supporting evidence that the model adds within-oblast timing signal.
3) Do not compare raw PR-AUC across groups or regimes. Frontline at-risk base rate is 0.479 vs rear 0.088, and Boyd's unachievable region makes raw AP rise with prevalence. Keep PR-AUC / base rate (already in metric_table), and say that it is still not fully prevalence-free (the floor is not linear in prevalence). This matters most for the D-015 before/after comparison, where the base rate changes with the reform.
4) Pooled PR-AUC is dominated by the high-prevalence frontline rows (McDermott Theorem 3). Overall model PR-AUC (0.466 validation) mainly reflects frontline performance. Report PR-AUC per group, and optionally an unweighted within-unit mean AP / unit base rate.
5) Report the within-unit selection explicitly. The within-unit mean currently drops 8-10 units (min 10 positives and 10 negatives), including Kharkivska and Dnipropetrovska. Print the dropped list next to the number (metric_table already stores it) and consider a sensitivity row with min_class = 5, labelled post hoc, or a positives-weighted mean. Small-cluster c-indexes are noisy and too extreme (van Klaveren 2019), so also show the spread (min / median / max, or a per-unit table from reports/official/metrics_by_unit.csv).
6) Consider a cross-sectional 'within-hour' AUC (rank the oblasts at each forecast time t, average over t with at least one positive and one negative). It isolates the spatial-targeting skill that within-unit AUC averages out, so the three numbers (pooled, within-unit, within-hour) separate 'which oblast', 'when' and 'where, given a wave'. This is a suggestion from this review, not from a source, and it is post hoc on the test window, so label it as such.
7) Calibration: report calibration-in-the-large per group, not only overall. On the final test the overall -0.006 hides -0.075 frontline and +0.006 rear. Keep the plain binary objective (no class weights, no resampling) per van den Goorbergh 2022. If recalibration is ever fitted, fit it on validation only (D-021). Since group-level CITL errors have opposite signs, a single global Platt fit would not fix them; a per-group intercept fitted on validation would be the minimal option and needs the human's approval as a model change.
8) Uncertainty: per-unit and per-group AUC and Brier from 4-6 weeks of hourly, clustered data have iid standard errors that are too small (Wilks 2010). Use the D-013 week-block bootstrap for the model-minus-recent-rate gain, and do not claim significance from iid DeLong tests.
9) For the new-regime check (D-015 (c)), within-oblast AUC plus per-group calibration-in-the-large is the right pair: AUC tells whether the ranking transferred, CITL tells whether the level transferred. Raw PR-AUC changes would mostly reflect prevalence change.
best_practices: ADOPT: (a) A strictly proper score (Brier, BSS vs the strongest baseline) as the headline; rank metrics as secondary. (b) Report pooled AND within-unit ROC-AUC side by side, and treat a large gap as a sign that pooled AUC measures between-unit differences. (c) Report the within-unit eligibility rule and the excluded units with the number. (d) Report AP (step-wise, not trapezoidal) together with its prevalence, and the ratio AP / prevalence or PR-Gain when comparing settings with different base rates. (e) Per-group metrics whenever prevalence differs a lot between groups. (f) Calibration at the 'moderate' level (reliability curve) plus calibration-in-the-large per group. (g) Train on the natural class balance; fit any recalibration out of sample. (h) Dependence-aware uncertainty (block bootstrap) for clustered, autocorrelated rows. (i) Fix metric definitions before the test is opened. AVOID: (1) Calling a high pooled AUC 'skill' when a per-unit constant reaches the same value. (2) Choosing PR-AUC over ROC-AUC 'because the data are imbalanced' without a decision-based reason (McDermott 2024). (3) Comparing raw PR-AUC across groups, horizons (H = 1 vs H = 3) or regimes with different base rates. (4) Trapezoidal PR area via sklearn.metrics.auc(recall, precision). (5) Undersampling, oversampling, SMOTE or class weights when probabilities are the product. (6) An overall calibration number only, which can hide opposite-sign group errors. (7) iid confidence intervals or DeLong tests on hourly clustered data. (8) Adding new metrics after seeing the test results without labelling them as post hoc.
